title: Diabetes Type 2 - MedlinePlus
key_verified_facts: Type 2 diabetes is the most common form of diabetes where the body cannot use insulin properly (insulin resistance).
Over time, the pancreas cannot make enough insulin to keep blood glucose at normal levels.
Complications can affect the heart, blood vessels, nerves, eyes, and kidneys.
Healthy eating, physical activity, and weight loss are foundational to managing or preventing Type 2 diabetes.

title: Type 2 diabetes - Medical Encyclopedia
key_verified_facts: People with Type 2 diabetes may have no symptoms for years; it develops slowly.
Fasting blood sugar of 126 mg/dL or higher on two separate tests confirms diabetes.
Random blood sugar above 200 mg/dL with classic symptoms indicates diabetes.
Chronic high glucose leads to peripheral neuropathy, retinopathy, nephropathy, and peripheral arterial disease.

title: Type 2 diabetes - self-care
key_verified_facts: Daily self-care includes balanced meal planning, regular physical activity, and checking blood sugar as advised.
Foot care is essential: check feet daily for cuts, blisters, and redness; keep skin soft and dry carefully between toes.
Target blood pressure for most individuals with diabetes is under 130/80 mmHg.
Managing cholesterol and quitting smoking dramatically cut cardiovascular risk.

title: Hemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) Test
key_verified_facts: HbA1c measures average blood glucose over the past 2 to 3 months by evaluating glycated hemoglobin in red blood cells.
Normal: Below 5.7%.
Prediabetes: 5.7% to 6.4%.
Diabetes: 6.5% or higher on two separate occasions.
Target for many non-pregnant adults with diabetes is below 7.0%.

title: Type 2 diabetes - oral medicines
key_verified_facts: Oral diabetes medicines help lower blood glucose when lifestyle measures alone are insufficient.
Metformin is usually the first oral medication prescribed; it reduces liver glucose output and enhances insulin sensitivity.
Different classes work in different ways: stimulating the pancreas, blocking carbohydrate absorption, or eliminating glucose in urine.
Patients must take medications exactly as prescribed and report any hypoglycemia or side effects to their doctor.

title: Type 2 diabetes - what to ask your doctor
key_verified_facts: Routine visits should review HbA1c, blood pressure, weight, and medication effectiveness.
Annual checks include dilated eye examinations, microalbumin urine tests, and comprehensive foot exams.
Patients should prepare questions about individualized target ranges, sick-day rules, and emergency symptoms.

title: Diabetes Fact Sheet - WHO
key_verified_facts: Type 2 diabetes accounts for over 95% of all people with diabetes worldwide.
It was previously known as non-insulin-dependent or adult-onset diabetes, but is now seen increasingly in children and adolescents.
A healthy diet, regular physical activity, maintaining normal body weight, and avoiding tobacco can prevent or delay Type 2 diabetes.
Diabetes is a leading cause of blindness, kidney failure, heart attacks, stroke, and lower limb amputation.

title: Diabetes Health Topic - WHO
key_verified_facts: Diabetes is a chronic, metabolic disease characterized by elevated levels of blood glucose.
Over time, diabetes damages the heart, blood vessels, eyes, kidneys, and nerves.
Access to essential medicines, glucose monitoring, and patient education are key to preventing premature mortality.

title: Diabetes Q&A - WHO
key_verified_facts: Type 1 diabetes involves deficient insulin production and requires daily administration of insulin.
Type 2 diabetes results from the body's ineffective use of insulin, strongly linked to excess body weight and physical inactivity.
Gestational diabetes involves hyperglycemia recognized during pregnancy, associated with complications to both mother and infant.

organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
title: About Type 2 Diabetes - CDC
key_verified_facts: In Type 2 diabetes, cells don't respond normally to insulin; this is called insulin resistance.
The pancreas creates more insulin to compensate until it cannot keep up, resulting in elevated blood sugar.
More than 38 million Americans have diabetes, and about 90% to 95% of them have Type 2 diabetes.

organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
title: Symptoms of Diabetes - CDC
key_verified_facts: Classic symptoms: urinating often (especially at night), feeling very thirsty, losing weight without trying, and feeling very hungry.
Other symptoms include blurry vision, numb or tingling hands or feet, very dry skin, and slow-healing sores.
Symptoms of Type 2 diabetes often take several years to develop and can be mild enough to go unnoticed.

organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
title: Diabetes Risk Factors - CDC
key_verified_facts: Risk factors include being overweight or obese, being 35 or older, having a parent or sibling with Type 2 diabetes.
Being physically active less than 3 times a week is a significant modifiable risk factor.
History of gestational diabetes or delivering a baby over 9 pounds increases lifetime diabetes risk.
African American, Hispanic/Latino, American Indian, Asian American, and Pacific Islander groups face higher risk.

organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
title: Preventing Type 2 Diabetes - CDC
key_verified_facts: Losing 5% to 7% of starting body weight can cut Type 2 diabetes risk by more than half (58%, and 71% for age 60+).
Getting at least 150 minutes of moderate physical activity per week is a cornerstone of prevention.
Eating healthy foods with smaller portions helps maintain weight loss and normal glucose levels.

organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
title: Prediabetes – Prevent Type 2 Diabetes - CDC
key_verified_facts: Prediabetes means blood sugar levels are higher than normal, but not high enough yet to be diagnosed as Type 2 diabetes.
More than 1 in 3 US adults have prediabetes, and over 80% do not know they have it.
Prediabetes can be reversed through structured lifestyle change programs.

organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
title: Diabetes Testing - CDC
key_verified_facts: Fasting blood sugar test: Normal < 100 mg/dL, Prediabetes 100-125 mg/dL, Diabetes 126 mg/dL or higher.
A1C test: Normal < 5.7%, Prediabetes 5.7%-6.4%, Diabetes 6.5% or higher.
Glucose tolerance test: Normal < 140 mg/dL, Prediabetes 140-199 mg/dL, Diabetes 200 mg/dL or higher.
Random blood sugar: 200 mg/dL or higher with symptoms points to diabetes.

organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
title: Put the Brakes on Diabetes Complications - CDC
key_verified_facts: The ABCs of diabetes management: A = A1C test, B = Blood pressure (< 130/80), C = Cholesterol management, s = Stop smoking.
Keeping blood sugar in target range helps protect kidneys, vision, nerves, and heart.
Annual kidney, eye, and dental exams detect complications early before symptoms appear.

title: Type 2 diabetes Overview - NHS
key_verified_facts: Type 2 diabetes is a common condition that causes the level of glucose in the blood to become too high.
It is caused by problems with the hormone insulin and is often linked to being overweight or inactive, or having family history.
A lifelong condition, it can affect everyday life, but healthy eating and regular exercise help keep blood glucose stable.

title: What is type 2 diabetes? - NHS
key_verified_facts: Insulin is made by the pancreas and controls the amount of glucose in the blood.
In Type 2 diabetes, the pancreas does not produce enough insulin or the body becomes resistant to it.
Without treatment, high glucose levels can damage blood vessels and lead to serious heart and nerve problems.

title: Symptoms of type 2 diabetes & Urgent Advice - NHS
key_verified_facts: Symptoms include peeing more than usual (especially at night), feeling thirsty all the time, feeling very tired, and losing weight without trying.
Itching around the penis or vagina, cuts taking longer to heal, and blurred vision are common.
Urgent medical attention is required if there is severe vomiting, rapid breathing, confusion, or fruity-smelling breath.

title: Treatment & Lifestyle for type 2 diabetes - NHS
key_verified_facts: Initial management focuses on healthy food choices, keeping active, and losing weight.
Medications like Metformin and other tablets are introduced if lifestyle alone does not reach targets.
Some individuals eventually need insulin injections to keep blood glucose controlled.
Annual diabetic eye screening (retinal photography) and foot exams are standard.

title: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) - NHS
key_verified_facts: DKA is a life-threatening emergency caused by a severe lack of insulin leading to ketone buildup.
Symptoms include fruity-smelling breath, extreme thirst, frequent urination, deep rapid breathing, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and confusion.
Requires immediate emergency hospital treatment with intravenous fluids, insulin, and potassium.

organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK)
title: Type 2 Diabetes - NIDDK
key_verified_facts: Genes play a significant role in Type 2 diabetes by affecting insulin production and cellular response.
Excess visceral fat in the abdomen is directly linked to insulin resistance.
Type 2 diabetes cannot be cured permanently, but some people achieve remission with significant sustained weight loss.

organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK)
title: Risk Factors for Type 2 Diabetes - NIDDK
key_verified_facts: Individuals 35 and older, or those with BMI >= 25 (>= 23 for Asian Americans), should be screened regularly.
Having low HDL cholesterol below 35 mg/dL or high triglycerides above 250 mg/dL increases susceptibility.
PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome) is a major metabolic risk factor in women.

title: Understanding Type 2 Diabetes - ADA
key_verified_facts: Type 2 diabetes occurs when the body does not use insulin properly, causing high blood sugar.
Myth: Eating sugar alone causes diabetes. Fact: T2D is caused by a mix of genetics and lifestyle; sugary drinks contribute by adding excess weight.
Myth: Needing insulin is a failure. Fact: Beta-cell function naturally declines over time, making insulin a safe and appropriate next step.

title: Living with Type 2 Diabetes - ADA
key_verified_facts: The Diabetes Plate Method is the gold standard visual guide: 50% non-starchy vegetables, 25% lean protein, 25% quality carbs.
Carbohydrates are essential; eliminating all carbs is not recommended—focus on portion sizes and whole foods with fiber.
Ongoing self-management education empowers patients to prevent long-term microvascular and macrovascular complications.
